kcet|Chemistry|2016|55||0|0.s:
Dehydrohalogenation removes H and X across adjacent carbons to give an alkene, and the
slow step is breaking the C–X bond.
So the weaker the C–X bond, the faster the elimination.
Bond enthalpies fall steadily down the group, because the halogen's orbital grows larger and
more diffuse and overlaps the carbon 2p orbital less well:
C–F 485, C–Cl 327, C–Br 285, C–I 213 kJ mol⁻¹
C–I is the weakest and breaks most readily; C–F is the strongest and is hardest of all.
This also makes iodide the best leaving group and fluoride the worst — the same order governs
nucleophilic substitution.
∴ R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|56||0|0:
Set up the geometry. The internuclear axis is z, so the two nuclei lie along z.
For orbitals to overlap they must have regions of the same phase pointing at each other.
pₓ lobes point along x; p_y lobes point along y. The two are at 90° to each other and both are
perpendicular to the bond axis.
Take pₓ on atom A and p_y on atom B. Wherever the positive lobe of pₓ overlaps p_y, the negative
lobe of pₓ overlaps it by exactly the same amount.
The constructive and destructive contributions cancel precisely, so the net overlap integral is zero.
Zero overlap means no molecular orbital is formed and no bond results.
A π bond needs pₓ with pₓ, or p_y with p_y — parallel orbitals, not perpendicular ones.
∴ no bond is formed.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|57||0|0:
Count the σ bonds on each carbon; the number of hybrid orbitals needed equals the number of
σ bonds plus lone pairs.
Diamond — every carbon is bonded to four others in a tetrahedral network. 4 σ bonds ⇒ sp³,
angle 109°28′. All four valence electrons are localised, which is why diamond does not conduct
and is extremely hard.
Graphite — each carbon is bonded to three others in flat hexagonal sheets. 3 σ bonds ⇒ sp²,
angle 120°. The fourth electron sits in an unhybridised p orbital; these delocalise across the
layer, which is why graphite conducts and the sheets slide over one another.
Ethyne, HC≡CH — each carbon has 2 σ bonds (one to H, one to C) ⇒ sp, angle 180°, linear,
with two π bonds from the remaining p orbitals.
∴ sp³, sp², sp.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|58||0|0.s:
The mixture is described as miscible, so the two liquids form a single phase — there is no
interface to exploit.
(3) Filtration separates a solid from a liquid; there is no solid here.
(1) Sublimation needs a component that goes directly from solid to vapour; neither does.
(4) Crystallisation separates a dissolved solid from its solvent; again there is no solid solute.
(2) Distillation separates two miscible liquids by exploiting the difference in their boiling points.
Benzene boils at 80 °C and chloroform at 61 °C, a gap of about 19 °C, which is ample for a
simple distillation: the chloroform vaporises first and is condensed and collected, leaving the
benzene behind.
∴ distillation.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|59||0|0.s:
Divide each percentage by the atomic mass to get relative moles.
C : 40 / 12 = 3.333
H : 13.33 / 1 = 13.33
N : 46.67 / 14 = 3.333
Now divide through by the smallest, 3.333:
C : 3.333/3.333 = 1
H : 13.33/3.333 = 4
N : 3.333/3.333 = 1
So the simplest whole-number ratio is C : H : N = 1 : 4 : 1.
(Check the percentages add up: 40 + 13.33 + 46.67 = 100 ✓, so there is no oxygen to account for.)
∴ the empirical formula is CH₄N.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|60||0|0:
Nitration uses a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄. The sulphuric acid is
there to generate the electrophile, and it does so by protonating the nitric acid:
HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ ⇒ H₂NO₃⁺ + HSO₄⁻
H₂NO₃⁺ ⇒ NO₂⁺ + H₂O
The species that attacks the ring is NO₂⁺, the nitronium ion. It is linear, carries a full positive
charge and has an electron-deficient nitrogen, so it is a strong electrophile.
The benzene π cloud attacks it to give the arenium ion, and loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity,
giving nitrobenzene.
Note sulphuric acid is not consumed — it is regenerated when HSO₄⁻ takes the proton at the end.
NO₃⁻ (4) is an anion and could never attack an electron-rich ring.
∴ NO₂⁺.
kcet|Chemistry|2015|1||0|0:
Identify the crystal system from the pattern of edges and angles.
The conditions given are a ≠ b ≠ c with α = γ = 90° and β ≠ 90°.
So all three edges differ, two angles are right angles and exactly one is not.
Run through the systems:
Triclinic — a ≠ b ≠ c and *no* angle is 90°. Not this one, since two are.
Orthorhombic — a ≠ b ≠ c with *all three* angles 90°. Not this one, since β is not.
Tetragonal — needs a = b ≠ c with all angles 90°. Fails on both counts.
Monoclinic — a ≠ b ≠ c, α = γ = 90°, β ≠ 90°. Exactly the conditions given ✓
Monoclinic sulphur and Na₂SO₄·10H₂O are the usual examples.
∴ monoclinic.
kcet|Chemistry|2015|2||0|0:
On discharge, a lead storage battery turns **both** plates into PbSO₄:
negative plate  Pb + SO₄²⁻ ⇒ PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ (oxidation)
positive plate  PbO₂ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇒ PbSO₄ + 2H₂O (reduction)
Charging reverses both. Current is forced through the cell the other way, so each electrode
undergoes the opposite change:
the plate that was oxidised to PbSO₄ is **reduced back to Pb**
PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ ⇒ Pb + SO₄²⁻
and the other plate is oxidised back to PbO₂.
Using the battery's own labels — the negative plate is the anode while it discharges — it is the
PbSO₄ on that anode which is reduced to lead.
The sulphuric acid consumed during discharge is regenerated, which is why a charged battery
has the higher acid density.
∴ PbSO₄ on the anode is reduced to Pb.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|3||0|0.s:
The distinction turns on whether a phosphate group is present.
Nucleoside = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar
Nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate group
Adenosine is adenine joined to ribose through a β-glycosidic bond at C-1′ of the sugar. There is
no phosphate, so it is a nucleoside.
Add one phosphate at C-5′ and it becomes adenosine monophosphate, AMP — a nucleotide.
Options (2) and (3) describe the base alone: adenine is indeed a purine, but adenosine is the
base plus the sugar, which is more than just a base.
∴ adenosine is a nucleoside.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|4||0|0.s:
Orlon (also sold as acrilan) is polyacrylonitrile.
Its monomer is acrylonitrile, CH₂=CH–CN, which is also called vinyl cyanide — vinyl for the
CH₂=CH– group and cyanide for the –CN.
The polymerisation is simple addition across the double bond, initiated by a peroxide:
n CH₂=CH(CN) ⇒ –[CH₂–CH(CN)]ₙ–
The resulting fibre is used as a wool substitute in blankets and carpets.
For contrast: acrolein (1) is CH₂=CH–CHO, glycol (2) is a monomer of terylene, and isoprene (4)
is the monomer of natural rubber.
∴ vinyl cyanide.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|6||0|0.s:
Hydrogen peroxide can act either way, because its oxygen is at the intermediate state −1:
it can go down to −2 (acting as an oxidant) or up to 0 (acting as a reductant).
As an oxidising agent it works on all of these:
PbS + 4H₂O₂ ⇒ PbSO₄ + 4H₂O — the black sulphide becomes white sulphate, which is how old
oil paintings are restored.
Na₂SO₃ + H₂O₂ ⇒ Na₂SO₄ + H₂O
2KI + H₂O₂ ⇒ 2KOH + I₂ — iodide oxidised to iodine.
Ozone is the exception. O₃ is a far stronger oxidising agent than H₂O₂, so the roles reverse and
hydrogen peroxide is the one oxidised:
H₂O₂ + O₃ ⇒ H₂O + 2O₂
Here H₂O₂ gives up electrons and its oxygen goes from −1 to 0.
∴ H₂O₂ cannot oxidise O₃.
